characters: Ananse: a charming, expressive folkloric spider character walking upright with a round brown body, clever bright eyes, and a small woven kente sash.
Nyame: the majestic, kindly Supreme Creator in Akan tradition, with a silver beard and golden kente robes, seated on an Adinkra-carved golden stool in radiant heavenly light.
Aso: Ananse’s wise, warm-hearted wife wearing a colourful headscarf and wrapper inside their cosy earthen home.
Mmoatia: a small West African forest dwarf of Akan folklore—depicted as a compact, wingless, earth-toned forest dweller.

narrationPlan.voice: A lively storyteller; a booming, warm voice for Nyame and a quick, clever voice for Ananse
narrationPlan.pace: Lively storytelling, with a pause for each task (about 85 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A bright drum and a quick xylophone for Ananse (placeholder)
culturalNotes: In Akan and Ghanaian thought, Nyame (Onyame / Onyankopɔn) is the Supreme God, Creator of heaven and earth. Ananse climbs his web up to the heavens to petition Nyame, the Creator.

In the widely told Akan version, Nyame sets four tasks: Ɔnini the African rock python (Standard Twi Ɔnini; ASCII Onini), Mmɔborɔ, the stinging hornets (ASCII Mmoboro—their traditional Anansesɛm name, whereas kotokurodu is the everyday Twi word for hornet or wasp), Osebo (Ɔsebɔ) the leopard, and Mmoatia the forest dwarf (a small wingless West African forest dweller). Regional tellings vary in small details.

In the classic hornet episode, Ananse sprinkles water to mimic rain so Mmɔborɔ fly into an empty calabash gourd for shelter. Anansesɛm means “spider stories”, and the story reminds children plainly never to approach or trap real wild animals or stinging insects.

teacherGuide.overview: A retelling of the Akan tale of how Ananse climbed his web to the heavens and won Nyame’s stories, honouring Standard Twi names (Nyame the Creator, Ɔnini, Mmɔborɔ, Mmoatia the forest dwarf, Anansesɛm), noting regional variations, and reminding children never to trap wild animals.
learningGoals: Retell the four tasks set by Nyame, the Creator, in order.
Explain how Ananse and Aso used cleverness (such as the gourd and rain trick) instead of force.
Describe what a folktale (Anansesɛm) is and how tellings can vary.
beforeReading: Ask children what Anansesɛm (Ananse tales) they already know.
whileReading: Hold up four fingers as each task is named on page 2 (Ɔnini, Mmɔborɔ, Osebo, Mmoatia).
afterReading: Act out the story in four short scenes.
Ask an elder or parent for their version of how Ananse won Nyame’s stories and compare.
discussion: Why does the story say two minds are better than one?
Why must we never copy folktale tricks around real snakes, hornets, or wild animals?
reflection: Who do you ask for help when a task feels too big?

support: Use four picture cards for the four tasks (python, hornets in a gourd, leopard, forest dwarf).
stretch: Write the conversation between Ananse and Aso as they plan the rain-and-gourd trick for Mmɔborɔ.
